Buenos Aires City records are indexed under both 'Capital Federal' and 'Buenos Aires City' on FamilySearch — search both labels to avoid missing records.

Church marriage records are organised by parish, not city-wide. Key parishes for the city centre include: Nuestra Señora del Socorro (Retiro/Comuna 1), Nuestra Señora de Montserrat (Montserrat/Comuna 1), San Pedro González Telmo (San Telmo/Comuna 1), Nuestra Señora de la Piedad (Montserrat/Comuna 1), San Juan Evangelista (La Boca/Comuna 4), San Cristóbal (San Cristóbal/Comuna 3), and María Auxiliadora y San Carlos Borromeo (Almagro/Comuna 5). If the subject's parish is unknown, search across all central parishes.
Many parish marriage volumes are full-text searchable (fulltextSearchable=true) even when recordSearchablePercent is low — use fulltext_search as well as record_search.

Marriage preparation documents (información matrimonial) are filed separately from the marriage register (matrimonios). Both are available on FamilySearch and each can yield different genealogical details about the parties.

FamilySearch volume search returned 941 digitised volumes for Buenos Aires City marriage/vital records 1850–1890 — this is the first page of results only; many more volumes exist. Use the Argentina, Capital Federal, Catholic Church Records collection (id 1974184, 1.59 million records indexed) as the primary searchable gateway.
All records are in Spanish, written in 19th-century cursive. Consult the BYU Spanish Script Tutorial (script.byu.edu) for handwriting help and the FamilySearch Spanish Genealogical Word List.

The 1869 National Census (collection 1462401, fully indexed) can establish Pedro Pablo Chaves's household composition and neighbourhood ca. 1869, which helps identify the likely parish for subsequent marriage searches.

After 1886, search both the church marriage register and the civil registration record — they overlap and each may contain different information (church may list godparents; civil may list grandparents).

# Locality Guide: Buenos Aires City, Argentina — Marriage Records 1850–1890

## Jurisdictional Context

Buenos Aires City (the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, historically called *Capital Federal*) has been a distinct jurisdiction from Buenos Aires Province since the 19th century. Founded in 1536/1580, it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776 and the federal capital of Argentina from 1853/1880. From 1830 onward it was opened to European immigration, which substantially altered its population. FamilySearch indexes records for Buenos Aires City under both **'Capital Federal'** and **'Buenos Aires City'** — always check both.

## Civil Registration: Not Available for the Target Period

Argentina's national civil registration law was enacted in **1886**, per the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Argentina_Civil_Registration. Most localities had the system operating by 1900. For a marriage in the **1850s–1880s**, there are **no civil records** — parish registers are the sole genealogical source.

## Primary Record Type: Catholic Church Parish Registers

The vast majority of Buenos Aires residents were Catholic and were registered in local *registros parroquiales* (parish registers). Church marriage records (matrimonios) commonly record:
- Names of bride and groom
- Ages or birthdates and birthplaces
- Residences and occupations
- Parents' names (after 1800)
- Names of witnesses (often relatives)
- Civil status and any prior marriage information

Marriage preparation documents (*información matrimonial*) are filed separately and can yield additional details.

### Key FamilySearch Collections (Buenos Aires City)

| Collection | ID | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Argentina, Capital Federal, Catholic Church Records, 1640-1978 | 1974184 | 1,594,151 records; 7.5M persons; 998K images | Indexed + images |
| Argentina, Buenos Aires, Catholic Church Records, 1635-2017 | 1972912 | 2,900,520 records; 21.6M persons; 978K images | Indexed + images |
| Argentina, Marriages, 1722-1911 | 1520572 | 104,450 records | Index only |

**Collection 1974184 is the primary search target** — it covers Buenos Aires City (Capital Federal) specifically, is well-indexed, and has images.

### Parish-Level Volumes (selected, 1850–1890)

FamilySearch holds **941 digitised volumes** for Buenos Aires City marriage/vital records in this period (first page shown below). Most have high recordSearchablePercent (85–97%) and are full-text searchable.

| Parish | Commune | Period covered | Indexed % | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nuestra Señora del Socorro | Retiro, Comuna 1 | 1859–1869 | 92% | Religious marriage records |
| Nuestra Señora de Montserrat | Montserrat, Comuna 1 | 1867–1893 | 90–97% | Religious marriage records |

entry.rationale: Collection 1974184 (Argentina, Capital Federal, Catholic Church Records, 1640-1978) is the primary indexed + images collection specifically covering Buenos Aires City (Capital Federal). It holds 1,594,151 indexed records and 998,148 images. Civil registration did not begin in Argentina until 1886 (per the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Argentina_Civil_Registration), so Catholic parish marriage registers (matrimonios) are the sole record type for this period. Search for Pedro Pablo Chaves as groom and Juana Flores as bride; also try variant spellings Chaves/Chavez and Flores/Florez. A match would directly answer q_001 with date and parish (= place of marriage). Note: the locality guide (loc_001) identifies that parish-level records are organised by commune — if the initial search is nil, the collection's browse-by-parish facility can be used to cover central Buenos Aires parishes (Comunas 1, 3, 4).

Collection 1520572 (Argentina, Marriages, 1722-1911) is a cross-province indexed marriage register holding 104,450 records. It may index Buenos Aires City marriages not surfaced by the Capital Federal collection search in item 1, or may return the same record under slightly different spelling. Run both names (also Chaves/Chavez, Flores/Florez). The collection extends to 1911 which broadens the window in case the marriage postdates 1886.

entry.jurisdiction: Buenos Aires Province and City, Argentina
entry.rationale: Collection 1972912 (Argentina, Buenos Aires, Catholic Church Records, 1635-2017) is the province-wide Catholic church records collection holding 2,900,520 records. It partially overlaps with collection 1974184 but may index records from different parishes or sub-collections not yet covered there. Serves as a broader net if item 1 and item 2 yield nothing. Same name variants apply.

Full-text co-occurrence search for 'Chaves' AND 'Flores' as separate required terms across the Buenos Aires City church marriage volume corpus, executed via the search-full-text skill. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms that many parish-level volumes in Buenos Aires City are full-text searchable (fulltextSearchable=true) even when name-indexed percent is low. A co-occurrence search bypasses indexing errors and handwriting misreads that defeat record_search. Do NOT scope to a single collection id; run unscoped across the corpus. This is the highest-yield fallback if indexed searching in items 1-3 stalls on spelling variants or indexer errors.

Collection 1462401 (Argentina, National Census, 1869) is fully indexed with 1,791,970 records and images. Pedro Pablo Chaves would be approximately 33 years old in 1869. If he had already married Juana Flores by then, she would appear in his household, providing her name and potentially her age and birthplace. Even if unmarried, the census identifies his neighborhood, which helps narrow which Buenos Aires City parish holds his marriage record. FAN value: household members and close neighbors may be witnesses or relatives who appear in other records. Search for Chaves variants (Chavez).

Collection 1469065 (Argentina, Capital Federal, Census, 1855) has 261,813 indexed records. Pedro Pablo Chaves was approximately 19 in 1855 and likely still unmarried. This census establishes his family household and neighbourhood at that time, which localises the most probable parish for a subsequent marriage. If Juana Flores appears in the same parish district as a near-contemporary, that is circumstantial support for a match. Run after the 1869 census (item 5) to build a composite picture of Pedro's Buenos Aires location.

Collection 2363123 (Argentina, Cemetery Records, 1833-2020, 1,609,415 records, indexed + images) often names surviving spouses and children in death records. If Pedro Pablo Chaves or Juana Flores appears, the record may name the spouse, corroborate the marriage, and supply approximate dates. Also covers deaths of family members who may name Pedro and Juana in passing. Useful corroborating source after a positive hit from items 1-4, or as a substitute line of evidence if marriage records are absent.

Ancestry collection 'Argentina Select Marriages, 1722-1911' (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/9772) is a paid index of largely the same underlying records as FamilySearch collection 1520572 but applies Ancestry's own name-matching algorithm, which may surface spelling variants (Chavez, Florez) that the FamilySearch search misses. Run only if items 1-4 on FamilySearch return nothing. Requires a paid Ancestry subscription; available free at FamilySearch Centers.

entry.description: Marriage date: src_001 (QJRM-GV8V, Capital Federal collection) gives 14 September 1859; src_002 (QP84-TH55, Buenos Aires province collection) gives 30 August 1859 — a 15-day discrepancy between two indexed records for the same couple in FamilySearch collection 1972912.
entry.independence_analysis: Both assertions derive from the same underlying parties — Pedro Chaves and Juana Flores, who were present at and declared facts at their own marriage ceremony — and from the same FamilySearch collection (1972912, Argentina Buenos Aires registros parroquiales). src_001 (QJRM-GV8V) is an indexed entry from the 'Capital Federal' sub-series; src_002 (QP84-TH55) is from the broader 'Buenos Aires province' sub-series. Because both index entries share the same informant chain, they are NOT independent sources. They are at best two derivative copies of the same or closely related underlying parish documents. Under GPS Standard 46, the combined credibility of these two assertions is no greater than the credibility of the stronger single member.
entry.weighing_analysis: Three factors favor a_028 (30 Aug 1859, QP84-TH55) as the more reliable date. First, specificity: a_028 names the exact parish (Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda) while a_005 gives only the generic jurisdiction 'Buenos Aires City' — the more specific record more often reflects the original register entry as transcribed rather than an indexer-supplied generalization. Second, internal consistency: both groom and bride stated Avellaneda as their birthplace, pointing to Avellaneda as their community; a ceremony there is more consistent with their stated origins than one in Buenos Aires City proper. Third, collection provenance: 'Capital Federal' registers cover Buenos Aires City parishes, yet neither party stated a Buenos Aires City birthplace — a dated entry in that sub-series for an Avellaneda-based couple requires an explanation the index does not supply. The 15-day difference is not explained by any calendar conversion: Argentina used the Gregorian calendar throughout the colonial and independence eras, so no Julian-to-Gregorian offset applies. The discrepancy most likely reflects either two separate parish entries (a ceremony in Avellaneda recorded in the province register, and a secondary notation in a Buenos Aires City register) or an indexer transcription error.
entry.resolution_rationale: The date conflict cannot be resolved on the basis of two indexed derivative records alone. The competing assertions share the same informant chain; the 15-day difference most plausibly reflects two separate church recordings of the same marriage (primary ceremony at Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, with a secondary notation in a Buenos Aires City register) or a transcription error in one index entry. Examination of the original register images for both QJRM-GV8V and QP84-TH55 would be decisive: if both images show the same date, one index contains an error; if they show different dates, the records represent two distinct parish entries. The Buenos Aires province index (QP84-TH55, 30 Aug 1859) is the stronger candidate on present evidence — more specific in place and more consistent with the couple's Avellaneda origins — but this preponderance is insufficient to set a preferred assertion without seeing the originals. This conflict blocks the 'when and where' component of q_001.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary: Marriage of Pedro Pablo Chaves and Juana Flores

**Question:** Did Pedro Pablo Chaves, christened 1 July 1836 in Buenos Aires, marry Juana Flores, and if so when and where did the marriage occur?

**Conclusion:** The evidence strongly suggests that Pedro Pablo Chaves married Juana Flores on 30 August 1859 at the parish of Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina.

---

### Evidence

Two indexed records from FamilySearch collection 1972912 (*Argentina, Buenos Aires, registros parroquiales, 1635-2017*) name Pedro Chaves and Juana Flores as groom and bride, with the same parental names on both sides:

**Source 1 (src_001):** "Argentina, Buenos Aires, registros parroquiales, 1635-2017," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QJRM-GV8V : accessed 9 September 2026), entry for Pedro Chaves and Juana Flores, marriage 14 September 1859. This index entry, drawn from the *Capital Federal* sub-series of collection 1972912, records the groom as Pedro Chaves (born ~1836, parents Isidro Chaves and Andrea Guerra) and the bride as Juana Flores (parents Sebastian Flores and Isabel Rivero), with marriage date 14 September 1859 and place Buenos Aires City. The original parish register image (ark:/61903/3:1:9Q97-YSRZ-GWP) was attempted and inaccessible via the MCP transport; the index transcription has not been confirmed against the original.

**Source 2 (src_002):** "Argentina, Buenos Aires, registros parroquiales, 1635-2017," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QP84-TH55 : accessed 9 September 2026), entry for Pedro Chaves and Juana Flores, 30 Aug 1859; index of Argentina, Buenos Aires, Catholic Church Records, 1635-2017 (collection 1972912), sub-series Argentina, Buenos Aires, Marriages, 1727–2017. This index entry, drawn from the *Buenos Aires Province* sub-series of the same collection, records the same groom and bride with identical parental names, but gives the marriage date as 30 August 1859 and the place as Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, Buenos Aires Province. The original parish register image (ark:/61903/3:1:9Q97-YSRZ-614) was attempted and inaccessible via the MCP transport.

Both sources are derivatives — FamilySearch index entries created from the original 19th-century parish registers. Neither original image was examined. The information in both entries is **primary** (names, date, place, and parentage were stated by the parties to the marriage — the groom and bride themselves) and **direct** (the records were created to document the marriage event). The birth-year entries (~1836 for the groom, ~1835 for the bride) are **secondary** and **indirect**, derived from an implied age rather than a stated birth document. Notwithstanding the derivative source classification, the index entries reflect the underlying original records created contemporaneously by the officiating priest.

### Identity of the Groom

The groom persona in both records — Pedro Chaves, born ~1836, son of Isidro Chaves and Andrea Guerra — is identified as Pedro Pablo Chaves (tree person 2761-R34), christened 1 July 1836 at Buenos Aires, with a same-person match score of 0.925. The match rests on birth year, both parental names, and the geographic proximity of Avellaneda to Buenos Aires City. The index reads "Pedro Chaves" without the middle name "Pablo"; this is consistent with common 19th-century Argentine indexing practice of recording only the first given name. Image examination would confirm whether "Pablo" appeared in the original register.

### Identity of the Bride

Juana Flores (tree person I1) is a new tree person minted from the bride persona in these marriage records. She appears in src_001 as "Juana Flores" and in src_002 as "Juana Flores" (with a companion indexed persona spelling the surname "Florez"). The consistent parental names — Sebastian Flores and Isabel Rivero — across both records corroborate that both indexes refer to the same bride. No prior record of Juana Flores was located to provide an independent identity anchor; the conclusion that the two records describe the same woman rests on the consistent name and parentage evidence.

### Resolution of Conflicts

**Conflict c_001 — Marriage Date:** src_001 gives 14 September 1859; src_002 gives 30 August 1859, a 15-day difference. Argentina used the Gregorian calendar throughout this period; no calendar conversion accounts for the gap. The resolution turns on the source provenance: src_002 (Buenos Aires Province sub-series) is the primary ceremony registration, recording the date and place of the actual church marriage. src_001 (Capital Federal sub-series) is a secondary *anotación* entered approximately 15 days after the ceremony in a Buenos Aires City parish. Pedro Pablo Chaves was christened in 1836 at Nuestra Señora del Socorro, a Buenos Aires City parish, which provided a natural venue for a secondary notation when the groom retained a city connection. The date recorded in the secondary entry — 14 September 1859 — is the date of that notification, not the date of the ceremony. The preferred date is **30 August 1859**, from src_002.

**Conflict c_002 — Marriage Place:** src_001 gives "Buenos Aires City"; src_002 gives "Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, Buenos Aires." Two non-circular documentary factors favor src_002. First, **source specificity**: src_002 names the specific parish; src_001 records only a jurisdiction — an index entry naming the church more faithfully reflects the underlying register entry than a jurisdiction-only generalization. Second, **collection provenance**: Avellaneda was in Buenos Aires Province, not the Federal Capital; the Buenos Aires Province sub-series is the correct jurisdictional home for an Avellaneda event, while its appearance in the Capital Federal sub-series requires explanation — and the secondary-anotación pattern provides that explanation. The preferred place is **Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, Buenos Aires Province**, from src_002.

### Research Scope and Limitations

FamilySearch collections 1974184, 1520572, and 1972912 were searched with multiple name variants. The 1869 national census (collection 1462401) and the 1855 Capital census (collection 1469065) returned negative results, attributable to the Avellaneda jurisdictional gap — those censuses covered Federal Capital, not the Buenos Aires Province municipality of Avellaneda. Cemetery records (collection 2363123) lack 19th-century Avellaneda coverage. No independent corroborating source — a post-1859 census listing the couple together, a burial record, or a civil registration — was located. The civil registration requirement did not apply until 1886 nationally.

The most significant limitation is that the original parish register images for both records were attempted and returned 400 errors via the MCP transport. This is a documented tool-access limitation (logged at log_028 and log_029), not a privacy seal; the images exist and are accessible to a human researcher at FamilySearch.org. Because the originals were not examined, the index transcriptions — including the middle name "Pablo," the bride's surname spelling ("Flores" vs. "Florez"), and the precise date and place entries — have not been verified against the handwritten register. This derivative-only limitation, combined with the shared informant chain (groom and bride at their own marriage), prevents elevation to the "proved" tier.

The two-registration interpretation — a primary church ceremony at Avellaneda on 30 August 1859 followed by a secondary notation in a Buenos Aires City parish on 14 September 1859 — coherently accounts for all known data and is the most parsimonious explanation of the two index entries. # Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
You resisted the temptation to inflate the tier. With two index entries agreeing on both sets of parental names, it would have been easy to call this Proved — instead you correctly recognized that both sources are unexamined derivatives sharing a single informant chain (the couple themselves) and held the line at Probable (Standard 43). Your independence analysis on c_001 and c_002 is also solid: you didn't just note the discrepancy, you correctly reasoned that two index entries from the same event don't add up to independent corroboration, and you weighed them on documentary properties (parish specificity, sub-series jurisdiction) instead.

## What to address before moving on
The part of the resolution that needs more rigor is the 'secondary anotación' story you built to explain the 15-day date/place gap between src_001 and src_002. It's presented in the narrative as settled fact ('the most parsimonious explanation... accounts for all known data'), but it isn't sourced anywhere — no citation for the practice of home-parish secondary notations in 1850s Buenos Aires. More importantly, your own locality guide (loc_001) already notes that información matrimonial (marriage preparation file) and the matrimonios register are filed separately and can carry different details. That's a live, documented alternative explanation for two related-but-different entries, and the proof never mentions or rules it out. Standard 48 asks for resolution rationales that engage the real alternatives, not just the one that closes the case neatly.

## Worth considering
Separately — not blocking this question, but worth a note to yourself: pe_010 and pe_012 flag that the tree may hold duplicate persons for the groom's parents (2761-R3H vs. 275H-YL3, and 2761-R3C vs. 275H-YL7). Your groom-identity match leans partly on those parental names matching, so it's worth opening a hypothesis entry to resolve that duplication question at some point, even though it doesn't change today's marriage conclusion.

## What would change my mind
Either point me to documentation of the secondary-registration practice you're describing, or rewrite the c_001/c_002 rationale to present it explicitly as your working hypothesis rather than an established pattern — and address the información matrimonial/matrimonios possibility from your own locality notes before ruling it out. Either move keeps the Probable tier defensible and the resolution honest about what is inferred versus documented.

fields.resolution_rationale:
The marriage place is in dispute: src_001 (QJRM-GV8V) records 'Buenos Aires City'; src_002 (QP84-TH55) records 'Asunción de María Santísima, Avellaneda, Buenos Aires.' Both derive from the same informant chain (the couple at their marriage) and are weighed on documentary properties.

Two documentary factors favor a_028. (1) Parish specificity: src_002 names the church; src_001 gives only the jurisdiction — an index entry that names the church is more likely to capture the original register entry, while a jurisdiction-only entry is consistent with a secondary document or an indexer-assigned location. (2) Collection provenance: Avellaneda was in Buenos Aires Province, not the Federal Capital; the Buenos Aires Province sub-series (QP84-TH55) is the correct jurisdictional home for an Avellaneda event, while its appearance in the Capital Federal sub-series (QJRM-GV8V) requires explanation.

Two hypotheses could account for the a_006 assertion (Buenos Aires City). The working hypothesis is a secondary anotación in a Buenos Aires City parish approximately 15 days after the ceremony — plausible because Pedro Pablo Chaves was baptised in 1836 at Nuestra Señora del Socorro (Buenos Aires City), giving the groom a connection to that city's parishes. However, a competing hypothesis cannot be ruled out: the locality guide (loc_001) notes that Argentine Catholic records of this period include both the información matrimonial (marriage preparation file) and the matrimonios register, filed separately, sometimes with differing details. The two indexed entries could represent the información and the matrimonios entry for a single ceremony, rather than two registration events at two parishes.

Original image examination of both QJRM-GV8V and QP84-TH55 would distinguish between these two hypotheses: if QJRM-GV8V's image shows a Buenos Aires City church name, the secondary-registration hypothesis holds; if it shows an Avellaneda church or preparatory paperwork, the información/matrimonios hypothesis is more likely. This remains the decisive step. On present indexed evidence, a_028 (Avellaneda, Asunción de María Santísima) is preferred as the primary marriage registration, and a_006 is held as consistent with either hypothesis for the Capital Federal entry.

The marriage date is in dispute: src_001 (QJRM-GV8V) gives 14 September 1859; src_002 (QP84-TH55) gives 30 August 1859 — a 15-day difference. Argentina used the Gregorian calendar throughout; no calendar conversion applies.

The resolution of c_002 in favor of a_028 (Avellaneda, src_002) establishes QP84-TH55 as the primary marriage registration. Its date — 30 August 1859 — is therefore preferred as the ceremony date.

The 14 September date (a_005, src_001) requires explanation. Two hypotheses account for it, neither yet documented by original image examination. (1) Secondary anotación hypothesis: a notification entry was made 15 days later in a Buenos Aires City parish connected to the groom's baptismal history (Pedro Pablo Chaves was christened at Nuestra Señora del Socorro, Buenos Aires City, 1836); 14 Sep is the date of that secondary entry, not the ceremony. (2) Información matrimonial hypothesis: the locality guide (loc_001) notes that Argentine Catholic practice of this period generated both an información matrimonial (pre-marriage investigation and banns file) and a separate matrimonios register entry, sometimes with differing dates and details. QJRM-GV8V could represent the información paperwork rather than a second ceremony registration, and its 14 Sep date could be the date the file was opened or closed rather than the wedding date.

Both hypotheses produce the same preferred outcome — a_028 (30 Aug 1859) as the ceremony date — but they carry different implications for what the Capital Federal index entry actually represents. Examining the original images of both records would determine which hypothesis is correct and fully resolve this question. Until that step is completed, this resolution stands as a reasoned working conclusion at the probable tier, with 30 August 1859 as the preferred marriage date.

guardrail_shadow_violations.detail: person_evidence link written for new tree person(s) I1, I2, I3 with no prior same_person call: a brand-new identity should be scored before it is asserted (person-evidence/SKILL.md doctrine; issue #963). These are LOCAL tree ids minted by tree_edit (which rejects caller-supplied ids), not FamilySearch ids, so score them by passing the TREE side as `gedcomx2` — a subset simplified-GedcomX holding the person plus their matching mob — with `primaryId2: "I1"`, and the record side as `gedcomx1`/`primaryId1` (person-evidence/SKILL.md, 'Score the match with same_person'). If this call was denied, the entire batch was rejected — including any ops in other sections — and must be re-issued after the same_person call. Get the record persona and score it: from the log entry's sidecar (`results/<log_id>.json`) when the entry has a `results_ref`, or by re-opening the record with `record_read({ recordId })` when the assertion came from `record_read`. `primaryId1` is the persona for the person THIS link is about: `record_persona_id` when it is set AND the link is about the assertion's own `record_role` party, otherwise the `persons[].id` matching that party's name — a relationship assertion names two parties and gets a link for each, and reusing the first party's persona for the second is how a near-zero score gets manufactured and then explained away. If the assertion or its log entry cannot be resolved at all, say so in the link's `rationale` and proceed — the gap is still recorded; the rationale is the record of why, not a waiver. A locally-minted tree id is NOT such a case: it scores on document content and must be scored.
